description.en: R. Meir was a second century scholar whose teachings are quoted frequently in the Mishnah and throughout rabbinic literature. He studied under [Elisha b. Abuya](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/elisha-ben-abuya?tab=sources), [R. Yishmael](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/rabbi-yishmael-b-elisha?tab=sources), and [R. Akiva](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/rabbi-akiva?tab=sources). He later became the head of the court in Usha, until he [quarreled](https://www.sefaria.org/Horayot.13b.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with R. Shimon ben Gamliel. He was also known to have experienced many miracles.
description.he: רבי מאיר היה חכם יוצא דופן שלמד עם אלישע בן אבויה, עם רבי ישמעאל ועם רבי עקיבא. התמנה לאב בין הדין באושא, עד שהסתכסך עם רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. לאחר מכן יצא מן הארץ ולא שב אליה. מסופר שחווה ניסים רבים.

en.prompt: Rabbi Meir was known as a bridge between the two great schools of Jewish legal thought: the schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Eruvin explains that Rabbi Meir learned from both of these figures and taught the teachings of both schools.
en.ai_context: The two great schools of the generation before Rabbi Meir were Rabbi Ishmael’s school and Rabbi Akiva’s school. Rabbi Meir learned from both of them and served as a bridge between them.
en.ai_prompt: Rabbi Meir uniquely bridged the teachings of two great schools by studying under both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. The Talmudic tractate Eruvin, part of the Order of Festivals, discusses rabbinic enactments that expand the areas in which one can carry and travel on Shabbat.

en.title: The Influence of a Heretic
en.prompt: Rabbi Meir was a close pupil of Elisha ben Abuyah, whom the rabbinic sages called Acher after he became a heretic. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Chagigah wrestles with the fact that Rabbi Meir learned Torah from a heretic, wondering whether the relationship tainted the Torah he learned.
en.ai_context: Rabbi Meir continued to repeat the teachings of Elisha ben Abuya after the latter became an apostate. This text learns a lesson from a story in the Talmud about the results of that decision.
en.ai_prompt: The power of human speech can influence even divine actions. This story from the Talmud (Chagigah 15b) illustrates how Rabbi Meir's teachings were initially rejected but later accepted due to a defense by Rabbah bar Sheila.

en.title: The Voice Behind the Mishna
en.prompt: The rabbis of the Talmud assumed that Rabbi Meir's position was reflected in the anonymous rulings contained in the Mishnah, the earliest code of Jewish law. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Sanhedrin names the different sages whose positions are reflected in the anonymous rulings of various earlier texts.
en.ai_context: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that the anonymous voice of the Mishna is assumed to be Rabbi Meir, and that he learned from Rabbi Akiva.
en.ai_prompt: The anonymous voice of the Mishna is often assumed to reflect the opinion of Rabbi Meir, a tradition rooted in his learning under Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches that an unattributed mishna aligns with Rabbi Meir's views, highlighting the influence of Rabbi Meir and his fellow disciples of Rabbi Akiva.
